stories.headline: India announces ₹15,000 crore package for Nepal after Modi–Balen Shah talks
stories.dek: Prime Minister Balendra Shah's first bilateral visit abroad also produced eight MoUs, a new Ayodhya–Janakpur train and access to two more Indian ports for Nepal.
stories.summary: India announced a ₹15,000 crore package for Nepal, about $1.6bn, after Narendra Modi held talks with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah in New Delhi on Monday. The two sides signed eight MoUs and launched a cross-border train service.
body: India announced a ₹15,000 crore development assistance package for Nepal on Monday after Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, on Shah's first bilateral visit abroad since taking office in March.

Firstpost put the package at 240 billion Nepalese rupees, roughly $1.62 billion. BBC News reported it as $1.6bn. It follows floods in Nepal in August; Firstpost reported that they killed around 1,500 people, with a further 5,200 reported missing and presumed dead.

The two sides signed eight memorandums of understanding covering policing, forensic sciences, civil service training, traditional medicine, satellite communication, sustainable urban development, healthcare, and livestock and fisheries. Under one, Isro and Nepal's Ministry of Information and Communication will set up a satellite communication network using the South Asia Satellite.

The leaders jointly launched the Sarayu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh and Janakpur in Nepal. They laid the foundation stone for a new Integrated Check Post at Banbasa in Uttarakhand and inaugurated a motorable bridge between Dharchula in India and Darchula in Nepal.

In energy, they laid the foundation stone for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project and dedicated Phase II of the Motihari–Amlekhgunj Pipeline. A petroleum terminal at Jhapa, for the proposed Siliguri–Jhapa petroleum pipeline, also received a foundation stone.

Modi described the relationship as one of "kinship and unbreakable trust" rather than simple neighbourliness. He said India had kept supplying fuel, fertilisers and other essentials to Nepal despite disruptions to global oil supplies linked to the West Asia conflict. He also announced a start-up incubator, an innovation hub, an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology and an agro-industrial park in Nepal.
Shah said the ties "stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as the ocean". He said the outcomes must translate into prosperity for farmers, jobs for youth and new markets for entrepreneurs.

BBC News reported that Nepal also secured access to two more Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip, and that India agreed to make the Kathmandu–Bhairahawa–Lucknow air route bidirectional. Nepal did not get the wider access to Indian airspace it has sought for its Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports. Analyst Anil Trigunayat told the BBC the Pokhara airport "can pose certain security challenges for India".
BBC News said the border dispute was largely absent from the leaders' public remarks, though the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remained.
keyFacts: India announced a ₹15,000 crore package for Nepal, about $1.6bn, on Monday.
Eight MoUs were signed, covering policing, space, health and other areas.
The Sarayu-Kamala Express links Ayodhya in India with Janakpur in Nepal.
Foundation stone laid for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project.
Shah took office in March; this is his first bilateral visit abroad.
stories.background: Nepal, a landlocked country between India and China, depends heavily on India for trade. BBC News reported that allegations of political interference and an unresolved border dispute have often complicated ties. Shah, a former rapper, came to power after youth-led protests toppled his predecessor, KP Sharma Oli, who was widely seen as closer to China.
stories.whyItMatters: Nepal is rebuilding after the August floods, and the new transport, port and energy links affect trade and travel between the two countries.

stories.headline: Ukraine says drones sank Russian corvette Merkury at Libya's Benghazi naval base
stories.dek: Russia's Kremlin warned of a 'dangerous trend' in attacks on its ships, while both of Libya's rival governments condemned the strike on their territory.
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit a cargo ship off Libya on Sunday. The Kremlin warned of rising tensions but did not comment directly on the Libya strikes.
body: Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit a second Russian vessel at Libya's Benghazi port on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a statement on Monday.

Zelensky said seven Ukrainian-made naval drones were used. A Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette, he said. The second target, he said, was the dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which he said Russia used to transport weapons. He called the operation "exemplary" and thanked the Security Service of Ukraine and the Defence Forces.

Local authorities said an explosion hit a warship in the early morning at the Benghazi naval base as it docked for fuel and supplies before returning to Russia. The local health ministry said it received injured people from a commercial ship targeted off the port. It is unclear whether that is the vessel Ukraine named.
BBC Verify geolocated videos showing a ship engulfed in flames and smoke. Planet Labs satellite imagery showed a boat on fire at the port at 05:47 GMT.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not comment directly on Libya. He said information would come from Russia's Defence Ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it". He called the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" a "dangerous trend" leading to "an escalation of tensions in the region".

Libya's two rival governments both condemned the attack. The Tripoli foreign ministry said Libya would not be drawn into the conflict and that foreign forces would not be allowed to use its ports for military purposes. The eastern government in Benghazi called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on its sovereignty.

The eastern Government of National Stability said the Russian ship was using the port under an existing maritime agreement. It accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity of hosting Ukrainian military personnel. Eastern prime minister Osama Hamad said he asked the United Nations to investigate suspicions that the boats were launched from western Libya. Tripoli did not immediately respond to Fox News, and it warned separately against hosting foreign forces.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".

The strike followed a Saturday drone attack on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland. Finland's military said Ukraine was likely responsible. Kyiv has not commented on that incident.
keyFacts: Zelensky said seven naval drones sank the corvette Merkury at Benghazi on Sunday.
He said a Ka-27 helicopter was destroyed and cargo ship MV ANGARA was hit.
Libya's Tripoli and eastern governments both condemned the attack.
The UN mission in Libya called for an independent investigation.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km from Moscow, according to the BBC.
stories.background:
Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, with a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east. The Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east, has longstanding links with Russia. Neither administration has formally taken a side in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped at Benghazi for several days under a cooperation agreement. In March, Russia's Transport Ministry alleged Ukrainian drones launched from Libya attacked the tanker Arctic Metagaz. Kyiv never claimed that attack.
stories.whyItMatters: The strike places a Libyan port at the centre of the Russia-Ukraine war and prompted both Libyan governments and the UN to warn against involving the country in foreign conflicts.

stories.headline: COP31 ends in Antalya with no agreement after EU and others reject final text
stories.dek: The longest UN climate summit on record closed without a deal because the draft made no direct mention of fossil fuels, and Saudi Arabia was accused of leading resistance.
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday without a deal after the EU, Panama and others refused a draft text that did not mention fossil fuels. It ran two days past schedule, making it the longest UN climate conference.
body: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended late on Sunday without a main political agreement after the European Union, Panama and other countries refused a draft that did not mention fossil fuels.

The talks were due to close on Friday and ran about 48 hours over, making them the longest UN climate conference on record. BBC News said it was the first time since Copenhagen in 2009 that a COP's main political agreement collapsed in this way.

Decisions at the talks need consensus. The objections of countries including EU members, Panama, Belize, Vanuatu, the UK, the Marshall Islands and Norway meant the "Antalya pact" could not be adopted, the Guardian reported. The Hindu reported the EU position was backed by about 130 countries.

The only indirect reference to fossil fuels in the text was a nod to the COP28 pledge of 2023 to "transition away" from them in energy systems. Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, said: "We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel." Panama's chief negotiator, Ana Aguilar, called the text "a setback, a rollback".

India, China, Saudi Arabia and other members of the Like Minded Developing Countries group did not object to the text, though they voiced concerns about adaptation finance and equity. India's Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said "climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation". Ghana, which accepted the text, said Africa "has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it".

Saudi Arabia led the push against fossil fuel language and instead favoured carbon capture and storage, according to AFP via CNA. Its energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said at the summit: "What unites us is the goal, and not necessarily the path to reach it." O'Brien told AFP the conference was "hijacked by some oil states". CNA said the IMF forecasts a 3.3 per cent fall in Saudi GDP this year.
Poorer countries also objected that the draft set no figures for adaptation finance, nor a baseline for the pledge made at COP30 to triple it, BBC News reported.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed". Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co-hosted the talks, cited "difficult geopolitical times". Chris Bowen, Australia's minister and president of negotiations, spoke of "unbridgeable red lines".

Some agreements were reached, including progress on a just transition mechanism for workers and communities. More than 80 countries backed Turkey's target for electricity to meet 35% of global energy use by 2035.

Al Gore called the process "in need of significant reform". UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek external advice on possible reforms. He defended consensus as having delivered the Paris agreement, but acknowledged it "fell short" on Sunday. The next conference, COP32, is scheduled for November 2027 in Ethiopia.
keyFacts: COP31 in Antalya ran about 48 hours past its Friday deadline, the longest UN climate summit.
The final draft did not mention fossil fuels directly; the EU, Panama and others rejected it.
Reports put the number of countries backing the EU stance at about 130.
Saudi Arabia was accused of leading resistance to fossil fuel language, which it favoured replacing with carbon capture.
COP32 is scheduled for November 2027 in Ethiopia.
stories.background: At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels. At COP30 in Brazil, they agreed to triple adaptation finance. UN climate decisions require consensus among all parties, so a single objection can stop a text.
stories.whyItMatters: Without an agreed text, the summit set no new collective direction on fossil fuels or adaptation finance for poorer countries. It has also prompted discussion of changing how UN climate talks decide.

stories.headline: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; shares jump about 33%
stories.dek: Trump says he persuaded the board to bring Huang back, while lawmakers from both parties demand answers and a Senate hearing is set for December 3.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, 11 days after he resigned over reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Shares rose about 33%, adding roughly $1 trillion in market value, while lawmakers pressed for hearings.
body: Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive, effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nvidia shares rose about 33% by midday in New York, according to the BBC, adding roughly $1 trillion to the company's market value. The tech-heavy Nasdaq gained nearly 7%. Micron rose 19% and Intel nearly 13%. Even so, Nvidia's share price remains about 21% below its level a month ago, the BBC reported.

In a statement, the board said it reached its decision after "a series of discussions and meetings" with Huang. It said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and was confident his return "poses no national security risk". Board chair Harvey Jones said reinstatement was in the interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers.
Huang said he was honoured to return. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as chief financial officer, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

CNBC, citing anonymous sources, reported that senior government officials briefed the board late last week and said no national security laws had been violated. Huang and the board held their first talks since his exit on Saturday and agreed on his return at a second meeting on Sunday, those sources said. They added that the falling share price accelerated the talks.

President Donald Trump told CNBC he had spoken to the board "directly and indirectly" and "convinced them". He said the board asked for assurance on national security and the administration gave it "with everything we know". In a social media post, Trump said the government had no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

Lawmakers from both parties criticised the decision. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, called it "reckless" and said Nvidia still owes Congress answers on export-control compliance. Republican Sen. John Cornyn asked on X: "No national security risk? Based on what?" Republican Rep. Don Bacon said Congress must find out who approved high-end chip sales to China.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Democrats would investigate any wrongdoing by the administration, Huang or other Nvidia executives.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott said Huang will testify publicly on December 3 as the sole witness. Huang is also due for a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, and general counsel Tim Teter on December 2. The board said an investigation by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz will continue to conclusion.
keyFacts: Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang, effective immediately.
Shares rose about 33%, adding roughly $1 trillion in market value, the BBC reported.
Huang is due before three House committees on December 1 and the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.
Colette Kress, interim CEO, stays on as chief financial officer.
stories.background: Huang resigned earlier this month after reports of multiple extramarital affairs. The New York Times reported on Sunday that one woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during part of the relationship. The board had said for weeks it was not considering his return, and set up an independent committee to investigate. Huang has opposed strict export controls on advanced chips.
stories.whyItMatters: Nvidia's chips are central to the AI industry, and its share price moved markets broadly. Congressional hearings will examine export-control compliance and what the government told the board.

perspectives.summary: The board says Huang's return poses no national security risk and serves shareholders. Trump says he convinced the board and that the government has no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang.

perspectives.label: Lawmakers of both parties
perspectives.summary: Warren, Schumer, Cornyn, Bacon and others say national security questions remain unanswered. They want to know what the government told the board and are pushing export-control legislation.

perspectives.label: Investors and tech figures
perspectives.summary: Elon Musk said the board's "mistake has been corrected". Market analysts told the BBC that Huang has a "talismanic influence" over the sector.

stories.headline: Iran vows 'all available means' against US blockade as Treasury targets its finances
stories.dek: The US Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses and front companies on Monday, and a separate report flagged nearly $15bn moving through possible shadow banking networks.
stories.summary: Iran's Foreign Ministry said on Monday it would use all available means against the US naval blockade. The same day the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian exchange houses and overseas front firms and flagged nearly $15bn in possible shadow banking flows.
body: Iran said on Monday it would use all available means to counter a US naval blockade, while the US Treasury announced new sanctions on Iranian exchange houses and overseas front companies it accuses of moving billions of dollars for Tehran.

"We will certainly not tolerate these actions and will use all available means to counter U.S. aggression," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly press briefing. He described the sanctions, economic blockade and naval blockade as "an act of military aggression against Iran" and said Iran was entitled under Article 51 of the UN Charter to use any means to defend itself.

Baqaei said Hormuz could be open within two days, but only if Washington agreed to Iran's list of demands, which includes lifting the blockade. "If the American side fulfils its commitments, security can be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the region in the shortest possible time," he said.

The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned more than two dozen exchange houses, front companies and financial operatives, according to Fox News. Treasury says they ran a "shadow banking" network spanning Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey that lets Tehran bypass US restrictions, sell oil and petrochemicals, and settle deals in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan.

Targets include the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, 10 front companies in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong, and Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company with three of its officials. Any US-based assets of those designated are frozen, and Americans are barred from dealing with them. Treasury also warned that foreign banks risk losing access to US correspondent accounts if they knowingly facilitate significant transactions for the networks.
"Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Separately, a report from Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) found nearly $15 billion moved through potential Iranian shadow banking networks since January 2025, the New York Post reported. At least $2.6 billion came from banks in China, $981 million from Singapore and $922 million from the UK, routed to institutions in the UAE. The report covered transactions before Operation Economic Outcast began in late August 2026.

Also on Monday, a judiciary official, Hassan Abdolianpour, told state television Iranian courts had awarded $290 billion in damages against the United States for decades of US actions, according to France 24. He said lawsuits had also been filed against Gulf Arab states accused of letting their territory be used for attacks on Iran.
Diplomacy remains stalled since the collapse of a June deal, The Hindu reported.
keyFacts: Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei spoke on Monday, November 23.
Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front firms and operatives.

War began on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
stories.background:
War broke out between Iran and the United States on February 28, when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Iran retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region, and groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq joined the fighting.

Iran has tried to block the Strait of Hormuz, and the US responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports, sanctions and a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran. A June deal meant to lead to a permanent settlement has collapsed.
stories.whyItMatters: The Strait of Hormuz is vital to global energy supplies, and the standoff over it has stalled diplomacy. Foreign banks and brokers dealing with Iran face added risk of US penalties.

perspectives.summary: Tehran says the blockade and sanctions amount to military aggression and that it may use any means in self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter. It says Hormuz could reopen if the US meets its demands.

perspectives.summary: Treasury says it is dismantling illicit networks that fund Iran's military, weapons programmes and proxies, and Bessent calls the shadow banking system the regime's last financial lifeline.

stories.headline: Supreme Court tells Bengal SIR tribunals to hear deleted voters' appeals first
stories.dek: The bench also told the Election Commission to add tribunals and find new premises in Kolkata, and asked for priority hearings for voters within Kolkata Municipal Corporation limits.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday directed West Bengal's SIR appellate tribunals to hear appeals by deleted voters first and defer appeals against inclusions. It also ordered the Election Commission to increase the number of tribunals.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing challenges to West Bengal's special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls to take up appeals by deleted voters first, and to defer appeals against the inclusion of other voters for the time being.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana told the tribunals to sort appeals into two groups. The first covers voters whose names were deleted. The second covers appeals against the inclusion of certain voters. The court said the second set "does not involve any urgency".
According to figures placed before the court, 38.31 lakh appeals have been filed. Of these, 22.21 lakh seek restoration of deleted names and 16.10 lakh challenge inclusions.

The bench ordered that appeals by deleted voters in constituencies within Kolkata Municipal Corporation limits be given priority because of the coming municipal elections. The Hindu, as cited by Scroll, reported that the court wanted these heard within a week. Scroll reported that the polls are expected before December 7.

The court directed the Election Commission of India, in consultation with the chief justice of the Calcutta High Court, to increase the strength of the tribunals. It also asked the commission to identify alternative premises in Kolkata. Scroll, citing the order, reported the sites should be in central Kolkata or near the airport.

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for the petitioners, said that only a little over one lakh of the nearly 38 lakh appeals had been decided. He said 93% of those decided had gone in favour of deleted voters. He added that more than two lakh voters in the Kolkata municipal area had been excluded and their appeals were pending.

The bench issued the directions while hearing submissions on the 16.10 lakh appeals filed by officials of the West Bengal chief electoral officer's office against inclusions. Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan questioned their legal basis. He argued that the CEO had no authority to file challenges in the commission's name against decisions of electoral registration officers. He said Rule 23 allows such appeals to go to an officer designated by the commission.

The Election Commission said in an October affidavit that officers of the CEO's office filed the appeals in their statutory capacity under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and that the matters had not come before the commission. Hindustan Times reported that the affidavit did not name anyone who authorised the filings.
keyFacts: Of 38.31 lakh appeals, 22.21 lakh seek restoration of deleted names.
16.10 lakh appeals challenge the inclusion of voters; the court deferred these for now.
Prashant Bhushan said about one lakh appeals were decided, 93% in favour of deleted voters.
The bench was headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
stories.background: The appellate tribunals were set up after a Supreme Court order on March 10, with former High Court chief justices and judges hearing appeals against exclusions, according to Scroll. They began hearing appeals in April. In September, the Election Commission told the court it was considering raising the number of tribunals to 42. The SIR began in June 2025, and in May the Supreme Court upheld its legality while saying the commission cannot decide citizenship.
stories.whyItMatters: Voters deleted from the rolls, including more than two lakh in the Kolkata municipal area according to the petitioners, may get their appeals heard before the municipal elections.

perspectives.label: Petitioners
perspectives.summary: Petitioners said very few appeals have been decided and most of those went in favour of deleted voters, so pending deletion appeals should be heard first. They also questioned the legal basis of the 16.10 lakh appeals filed by CEO office officials.

perspectives.label: Election Commission
perspectives.summary: In an October affidavit, the commission said CEO office officers filed the inclusion appeals in their statutory capacity under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and that the matters had not been brought before it.

stories.headline: Israeli strikes kill at least three in Gaza, including UNRWA worker
stories.dek: Oxfam separately reported that more than 99% of Gaza shows signs of environmental contamination, a finding the Israeli embassy in the UK rejected.
stories.summary: Israeli airstrikes killed at least three people in Gaza on Monday, including a UNRWA worker at a water well in Jabalia, the agency and medics said. Oxfam also published a report calling the territory a 'toxic wasteland'.
body: Israeli airstrikes killed at least three people in Gaza on Monday, November 23, including a man working for the UN Palestinian refugee agency UNRWA, the agency and local health officials said.

Medics named the UNRWA worker as Adel Al-Helo. He was working near a water well in the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza when he was killed, the agency and medics said. Three other people were wounded.

An UNRWA spokesperson told Reuters that initial reports indicated the strike hit a target on the street near the well, which was staffed by UNRWA employees and a guard. "The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations," the spokesperson said.

The Israeli military said it was checking the report when Reuters asked for comment. Helo's brother Nizar said he had worked at the agency for 35 years and had gone to run the well to supply residents of the camp with water.
Later on Monday, another Israeli strike hit a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.

Separately, Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory published a report saying more than 99% of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks. The report, based on satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data, cites heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos, dioxins and biological contaminants.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact would have "fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival". He accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza". Report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC she expected long-term health effects, including respiratory diseases, cancers and birth defects.

The Israeli embassy in the UK said the report "falls short of professional standards". It argued the study relied on satellite imagery and unverified assumptions and ignored the effect of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels dug by Hamas. Israel has rejected genocide accusations at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted.
The report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment in Gaza before any clean-up, with special attention to the protection of workers.
keyFacts: Adel Al-Helo, an UNRWA worker of 35 years, was killed near a water well in Jabalia camp.
A second strike on a vehicle in western Gaza City killed two people, medics said.
At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, per respective tallies.
Oxfam says more than 99% of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination.
All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza are out of operation, according to the BBC.
stories.background:
A US-backed ceasefire in October 2025 halted major fighting in Gaza but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas's disarmament. Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of the territory, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire.

Israel says its campaign is self-defence after the Hamas-led attack of October 2023, in which 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 taken hostage. The Hamas-run health ministry says at least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the war began; the UN considers its figures reliable.
stories.whyItMatters: Strikes continue to kill civilians and aid workers under the ceasefire, while Oxfam says contamination threatens the health of Gaza's residents for decades. Israel has tied large-scale reconstruction to Hamas's full disarmament.

perspectives.label: Israel
perspectives.summary: The Israeli military said it was checking the report of the UNRWA worker's death. The embassy in the UK called the Oxfam report methodologically flawed and said Israel acts in self-defence.

perspectives.label: Oxfam, UNRWA and Palestinian voices

stories.headline: Section 144 imposed in Madurai as Tamil Nadu seeks review of Deepam order
stories.dek: The state government has asked the Supreme Court to review its November 20 order allowing a one-time lamp lighting at Thiruparankundram on November 24, and Congress and BJP leaders have exchanged accusations.
stories.summary: Madurai authorities imposed prohibitory orders ahead of November 24, when the Supreme Court has permitted a one-time lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram. The Tamil Nadu government has filed a review petition, and Congress and BJP leaders traded accusations on Monday.
body: Madurai District Collector Nishant Krishna imposed prohibitory orders across the district on Monday night, ahead of the Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram Hill on November 24, according to News18.

The orders were issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which replaced Section 144 of the CrPC. They bar public gatherings, demonstrations, processions and climbing the hill from the night of November 23 until the morning of November 25, News18 reported. It said authorities acted over fears of large-scale mobilisation and possible clashes.

The Tamil Nadu government has filed a review petition against the Supreme Court's November 20 order, The Times of India reported. A bench led by Justice Aravind Kumar had permitted a strictly conditional, one-time lighting of the lamp at the Deepathoon, a stone pillar on the hill, on November 24. The petition seeks an immediate stay of that order.
The Hindu reported on Monday that a Tamil Nadu government report concluded that the structure on the hilltop is a survey pillar. Only the headline of that report was available to Meridian.

Congress MP Manickam Tagore told ANI that the government wanted to protect communal harmony. He accused the RSS, Hindu Munnani and the BJP of trying to create communal tension. "In Thiruparankundram, the Deepam will be lit," he said.

BJP leaders criticised the review petition. Chief spokesperson Narayanan Thirupathy called it "nothing but the appeasement of minorities". State vice president P Kanagasabapathi said the government was not willing to implement the court's judgment.

State secretary Vinoj P Selvam said that if the government could not handle "a small law and order situation", chief minister Vijay should resign. AIADMK spokesperson Kovai Sathyan said there was no difference between the DMK and the TVK.
The Supreme Court's order did not set a precedent or settle the wider claims over ownership and customary rights, The Times of India reported.
keyFacts: Madurai collector's prohibitory orders run from the night of November 23 to the morning of November 25.
The Supreme Court on November 20 allowed a one-time lamp lighting at the Deepathoon on November 24.
The Tamil Nadu government has filed a review petition seeking a stay of that order.
A state government report says the hilltop structure is a survey pillar, according to The Hindu.
stories.background:
The dispute concerns the annual lighting of the Karthigai Deepam at the Deepathoon on Thiruparankundram Hill, near the Sikandar Badhusha Dargah. In November 2025, local authorities withheld permission, citing law and order and the site's proximity to the dargah.

In December 2025 a single judge of the Madras High Court directed the temple authorities to light the lamp, noting the pillar was more than 50 metres from the dargah. A division bench upheld this on January 6, 2026. The state challenged the rulings in the Supreme Court, which issued notice in August 2026.
stories.whyItMatters: The prohibitory orders restrict movement and assembly in Madurai district for about two days around the festival, while the legal status of the lamp lighting remains unsettled.

stories.headline: Democrats win biggest US House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
stories.dek: Chuck Hubbard's 330-vote recount win over Virginia Foxx lifts the party to at least 258 seats, with four races undecided and Democrats also holding the Senate.
stories.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Virginia Foxx in North Carolina after a recount, giving his party at least 258 House seats, its most since 1992. Democrats are already setting up 2028 presidential debates.
body: Democrats have won their largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th District by 330 votes, according to the BBC.

The race was called on Sunday after a recount, which Foxx requested. State law allows one when the margin is under 1%. Foxx had held the seat since 2005. Hubbard lost to her by nine percentage points two years ago.

Democrats have now won at least 258 House seats to the Republicans' at least 173, with four races uncalled, the BBC reported. In 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency, Democrats also won 258 seats. The party will hold 56 of the 100 Senate seats when the new Congress convenes in January, CNA reported, citing AFP.

The uncalled races are in Tennessee and Minnesota, and two Louisiana contests go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's 4th District, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes. In Minnesota's 1st, Democrat Jake Johnson leads by fewer than 500.
NPR reported that Democrats took 56% of the House vote against 42% for Republicans, a 14-point gap it described as the party's largest margin in 50 years.

Hubbard said he had spoken to Foxx, who he wrote had "graciously conceded following the results of the recount process". Foxx said in a statement that she was "humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Hubbard told the BBC: "I think the American people are just sick of what's going on and they wanted a change." He said he would work with other lawmakers to hold President Donald Trump accountable. The BBC said Hubbard campaigned on the cost of living during the war with Iran. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have suggested war-related inflation was probably to blame for Republican losses, it reported.

Democrats may use their majorities to investigate conflicts of interest involving the president and those close to him, the BBC said. The Senate can also confirm or block cabinet and judicial nominations. Trump can veto legislation, and CNA noted that most major bills need 60 votes to clear procedural hurdles in the Senate.

Not every Republican lost ground. Rep. Cliff Bentz, Oregon's only Republican in the House, won a fourth term with 61% of the vote, Fox News reported. He said Republicans in the minority should highlight what he called the economic costs of Democratic policies. "I think that's hugely important, and that's what I'll be doing in these next two years," he said.
On Monday the Democratic National Committee announced 12 primary debates for the 2028 presidential nomination, five in 2027 and seven in 2028. The first is scheduled for June next year.
keyFacts: Chuck Hubbard beat Rep. Virginia Foxx by 330 votes in North Carolina's 5th District after a recount.
Democrats have won at least 258 House seats; Republicans at least 173; four races are uncalled.
Democrats will hold 56 of 100 Senate seats when the new Congress convenes in January.
The DNC plans 12 presidential primary debates, the first in June 2027.
stories.background: Foxx had represented North Carolina's 5th District since 2005 and earlier spent a decade in the state Senate. The 258-seat total matches the Democratic haul in 1992. Trump is term-limited, so Republicans must find a successor candidate for 2028.
stories.whyItMatters: Democratic control of both chambers gives the party power to investigate the administration and to block or confirm nominees, though Trump's veto and the Senate's 60-vote threshold limit what it can pass.

perspectives.label: Democrats
perspectives.summary: Hubbard said voters wanted change and that he would help hold Trump accountable. DNC chairman Ken Martin said the party is "on offence" and will keep its "foot on the gas" for 2028.

perspectives.label: Republicans
perspectives.summary: Trump and Vance have suggested war-related inflation probably caused the losses. Bentz argued Republicans can recover by criticising Democratic economic and regulatory policy from the minority.

stories.headline: SP and Congress reach broad consensus on UP seats, final numbers due in days
stories.dek: Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya said the alliance would 'lose badly' in 2027, as the two parties prepare a second round of talks on Tuesday.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party and Congress said after a 15-minute first round in Delhi on Monday that they had a broad consensus on seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election. The BJP's Keshav Prasad Maurya said the alliance would lose.
body: The Samajwadi Party (SP) and the Congress said on Monday they had reached a broad consensus on an alliance for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly election, after a first round of talks in Delhi that lasted about 15 minutes. Both expect to finalise the deal within two to three days.
Neither side disclosed seat numbers. The talks were held at the Delhi home of Congress leader Pramod Tiwari, according to NDTV. The delegations will meet again on Tuesday.

SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav, who led his party's team, said the atmosphere was cordial. "We will soon finalise this alliance and inform you. We expect to complete the process within the next two to three days," he told reporters. UP Congress chief Aradhana Mishra called the talks "positive" and "satisfactory" and said: "I cannot talk about numbers at the moment, but there is consensus."

NDTV, citing sources, reported that the Congress handed over a list of at least 130 seats in the 403-member Assembly, with a claim to a seat in almost every district, including all seats in Amethi and Rae Bareli. It said Etawah and Mainpuri, the bastions of Akhilesh Yadav's family, were left out. The SP made no counter-offer and said it would discuss the list with Akhilesh Yadav first.

An SP leader told NDTV: "Hum seat ke mamle me risk nahi le sakte (We cannot take a risk when it comes to allocating seats)." The Times of India reported that Akhilesh Yadav has said seats should go to whichever partner is more likely to win them.

The Times of India cited Congress sources as saying the party hopes for more than 100 seats and has identified about 140-150 constituencies, with around 60 high-priority seats in Category A. The state Congress had earlier sought 200 seats; Akhilesh Yadav publicly said the demand was 181, which caused some unease in the Congress, the paper reported.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya said the alliance was "no problem for us" and that it was "going to lose badly". He said the BJP would win with a full majority and seek a third consecutive term.
UP minister Danish Azad Ansari called the INDIA bloc a failed experiment. BJP national spokesperson Shahnawaz Hussain said the Congress had contested the most seats last time but won only two.
The two parties will hold their second round of talks on Tuesday.

The Uttar Pradesh Assembly has 403 seats.
In 2024, the SP won 37 Lok Sabha seats in UP and the Congress six.

stories.whyItMatters: The seat split will decide which constituencies each party contests against the BJP in the 2027 Uttar Pradesh election.

stories.headline: Bangladesh says Sheikh Hasina will be jailed if she returns from India
stories.dek: State Minister Shama Obaed Islam said Dhaka expects India to honour the extradition treaty and hand back the former prime minister, who faces a death sentence.
stories.summary: Bangladesh's State Minister for Foreign Affairs said Sheikh Hasina will be arrested and jailed as soon as she tries to enter the country. Dhaka is seeking her extradition from India as Awami League protests and bomb attacks continue.
body: Bangladesh will arrest and jail former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters in an interview on Sunday, November 22.

"As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course," Obaed said. She added that Dhaka wants India to "honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict".

Hasina has lived in India since fleeing Dhaka in August 2024 as protests demanded her resignation. She faces a death sentence in Bangladesh, and her Awami League party is banned. She has planned a return in December and has sought a new passport and identity card, requests the government has rejected.
India's External Affairs Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, it said it was examining Bangladesh's extradition request.

Obaed said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back. She said Dhaka wants balanced ties with New Delhi that do not compromise Bangladesh's "dignity, self-respect and interests". "India needs to decide what kind of foreign policy they need to adopt for Bangladesh," she said.

The Awami League announced a week of protests and rallies this month in support of Hasina's return, ending in a nationwide lockdown on November 19. According to local media, police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and arson attacks on vehicles in at least 28 districts over the past 10 days. Several police officers and civilians were injured.

Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Hasina's "politically bankrupt political party". Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence.

In the same interview, Obaed said Dhaka is increasing diplomatic pressure on Myanmar over the return of Rohingya refugees, after the International Court of Justice ruled that the 2017 killings and sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces amounted to state-sponsored genocide. Myanmar has criticised the ruling and said Rohingya could return only "when situations permit". About 1.2 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh.

Hasina fled Dhaka in August 2024 and faces a death sentence in Bangladesh.
The UN has said as many as 1,400 people were killed in the 2024 unrest.

stories.whyItMatters: The dispute could strain Dhaka-New Delhi relations, since India hosts Hasina and has yet to respond to the extradition request. Her planned December return is also tied to continuing street violence in Bangladesh.

stories.headline: Pakistani operatives found in defence, CAPF WhatsApp groups; audit ordered
stories.dek: Separately, the Home Ministry's cybercrime wing has advised users to avoid official or sensitive work on WhatsApp Web and to log out manually after every session.
stories.summary: Security agencies have detected suspected Pakistani intelligence operatives in 13-14 private WhatsApp groups of CAPF and defence-civilian personnel, PTI reported citing officials. An audit of social communication platforms has been ordered.
body: Security and intelligence agencies have detected suspected Pakistani intelligence operatives in 13-14 private WhatsApp groups used by Central Armed Police Forces and defence-civilian officials, PTI reported on Monday, citing officials.

The agencies have ordered forces and defence civilian organisations to audit their social communication platforms, including the identified groups, and to remove members who cannot be identified. They have also directed that no official or classified information be shared on such platforms, officials said.

The suspected operatives are believed to have joined using spoofed or compromised Indian mobile numbers. Officials said the numbers stayed on as "silent members", monitoring chats and documents shared in the groups.

The threat has been classed as a "targeted" cyber espionage campaign against personnel in sensitive security roles, officials said. A senior officer, quoted by PTI, said: "The stipulated cyber hygiene guidelines have been reiterated and it has been directed that no official or classified information and data be shared over social media platforms in the wake of this incident."

The alert follows an earlier flag by officials about a suspected Pakistani operative posing as a DRDO scientist named 'Soniya' in a WhatsApp group of defence-civilian officials. Officials said some sensitive information is suspected to have been shared in that group in exchange for money.
News18 described the matter as a suspected espionage network that has triggered a nationwide security alert, and said the claims are under investigation.

Separately on Monday, the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) of the Ministry of Home Affairs, through its National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, issued an advisory on safe use of WhatsApp Web. It did not link the advisory to the group infiltration in the reports reviewed here.

The advisory said a live WhatsApp Web session could be misused to read messages, send messages while impersonating the account holder, and access contacts and group conversations. It said closing a browser tab or window does not end a session and users must log out manually.

It advised against exchanging government, organisational, financial or confidential information over WhatsApp Web, especially on office, shared or public computers. Where use is unavoidable, it suggested private browsing mode, and it asked users to check the Linked Devices section and log out of unrecognised sessions.

stories.background: The I4C had issued earlier warnings in June and August 2026 about WhatsApp account takeovers through malicious files, mainly targeting company executives and finance staff, according to Firstpost.

stories.headline: Saurav Das says he was stopped at Delhi airport from flying to London
stories.dek: The Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson said immigration officials told him his passport had been flagged; a Delhi Police official told Hindustan Times the force was unaware of the matter.
stories.summary: Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das said on Monday he was stopped at Delhi airport from flying to London for a lecture at Oxford. He blamed the Modi government; a Delhi Police official said the force was not aware of the matter.
body: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) spokesperson Saurav Das said on Monday that he was stopped at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport from boarding a flight to London, where he was due to give a lecture at the University of Oxford.

Das made the claim in a post on X, writing: "I have been stopped by this cowardly Modi Govt at the Delhi Airport from flying to London to deliver a lecture at the University of Oxford." The Indian Express reported that the post did not state the reasons authorities gave him.

In a video on Instagram, reported by Hindustan Times, Das said his flight was at 1:00 am and that the students' union of Oxford had invited him. He said he was told at the immigration counter that his passport had been flagged. He attributed the flagging to the government.

In a follow-up video message, reported by News18, Das said he had also been invited by Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Edinburgh to speak about the Cockroach Movement. He said Indian students had worked hard to organise the events.

A Delhi Police official told Hindustan Times that the police were not aware of the matter and that immigration officials were involved. News18 reported that the government had not responded to Das's allegations. No official explanation had been reported at the time of publication.
The CJP said in a post on X that Das was invited to address the Oxford Union. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke also shared Das's post and wrote that Das had been invited to speak at a conference at Oxford.

Das, along with co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka and founder Dipke, has been at the forefront of CJP campaigns, Hindustan Times reported. Das and Ranka were held in Tihar jail after entering the denotified protest site at Jantar Mantar on October 13. They were released on October 21 on personal and surety bonds of ₹50,000 each.

The government had not responded to the allegations, News18 reported.

Hindustan Times reported they were protesting alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls and raised slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

stories.headline: BRO says Sheshnag road work stays on existing tracks after video draws criticism
stories.dek: Kashmiri political leaders, a cleric and an environmental activist demanded the work near the glacial lake be stopped; the Border Roads Organisation called the video's claim of new works incorrect.
stories.summary: The Border Roads Organisation said on Monday that its work near Sheshnag Lake on the Amarnath route is confined to existing tracks and follows environmental safeguards. Leaders from several parties and a cleric called for a halt after a video showed an excavator at the lake.
body: The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) said on Monday that its widening work on the Amarnath Yatra route near Sheshnag Lake is confined to existing tracks and complies with safety norms and environmental safeguards, after a video of an excavator at the lake drew criticism.

The video was first posted on an Instagram account named 'Neeraj_excavator_lover', according to The Indian Express. It shows heavy machinery building a road near the lake, on the trekking route from Pahalgam to the Amarnath cave shrine, and appears to show soil being dumped on the lake's shore. The account holder has since deleted it. Hindustan Times described the video as purported.

In a statement, the BRO, which comes under the Ministry of Defence, said the circulating video's claim of new works was incorrect. It said that, based on experience of previous Yatras and a requirement for a wider road, it had begun widening tracks and stabilising vulnerable stretches "to ease congestion and allow safer passage". It said it ensures safe disposal of excavated material, protects natural drainage and minimises disturbance to surrounding terrain. The Indian Express reported that the BRO did not explain why earth movers were being used at such altitude.

Official sources told The Indian Express the work is part of widening and stabilising the existing track from Chandanwari in Pahalgam to the cave. The paper said there had been no official word from the government on using excavators in the zone.

Sheshnag is among 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir for glacial lake outburst flood potential. It lies at 3,590 metres and is reached by a 23-kilometre trek from Chandanwari, according to The Indian Express.

Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, Kashmir's chief cleric, called the visuals "very disturbing" and said the work "must be immediately stopped". He said improving facilities for pilgrims had never been an issue, "But not at the cost of our fragile ecosystem."

Mohit Bhan of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) called it a "crime against Hinduism and faith in nature". PDP president Mehbooba Mufti said she feared Kashmir would become "another Uttarakhand", and that raising the issue would draw accusations of opposing the Yatra. Congress leader Pawan Khera accused the government of playing with the faith of Hindus and Kashmiri Muslims.

CPI(M) leader M Y Tarigami said the lake is surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes, and that disturbing it was "an invitation to disaster". He asked for details of the project, the agency and the clearances, and for an inspection by glaciologists. Aga Ruhullah Mehdi said the mountains were "not BJP's real estate".

Apni Party chief Altaf Bukhari asked the authorities to clarify whether the video is genuine. National Conference MP Mian Altaf, who said he had not seen it, said Kashmir's lakes "must be saved". Activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat called it "a disaster".

stories.background: Sheshnag lies on the Pahalgam route to the Amarnath cave shrine. Hindu belief holds that Lord Shiva left his serpents there before proceeding to the cave. Critics cited recent glacier-related disasters in Nepal, and earlier ones at Kedarnath and South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim.
stories.whyItMatters: Tarigami said people downstream, including in Pahalgam and along the Lidder, would bear the risk if work at the high-risk lake caused a disaster. The BRO says the widening is meant to ease congestion and make passage safer for pilgrims.

perspectives.summary: They say heavy machinery near a high-risk glacial lake endangers a fragile ecosystem and a site sacred to Hindus and Muslims, and want work stopped, with project details and clearances made public.

stories.headline: Centre yet to announce Winter Session dates, 103 days after Monsoon Session ended
stories.dek: Parliament has not been prorogued since the Monsoon Session was adjourned on August 13, and Congress leaders have questioned the lack of clarity on the Winter Session.
stories.summary: The Centre has not announced dates for Parliament's Winter Session, 103 days after the Monsoon Session ended on August 13. Opposition leaders have questioned the delay; the government has offered no explanation.
body: The Centre has not announced dates for the Winter Session of Parliament, 103 days after the Monsoon Session was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026, according to data from the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs compiled by NDTV.

That gap is longer than the 25-year average of about 95 days between the end of a Monsoon Session and the start of the Winter Session, excluding 2020, when no Winter Session was held. It has already passed the gaps in 2025 (102 days), 2004 (97 days) and 2016 (96 days). The longest since 2000 were 126 days in 2017 and 123 days in 2018. The shortest was 66 days in 2007.

The Hindu reported that the Winter Session has been skipped only four times in India's parliamentary history. Each case was linked to exceptional circumstances: the Emergency, the premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Hindu also reported that Parliament has stayed unprorogued for more than 100 days, a record, and that speculation has grown about a short special session to consider a delimitation Bill.

Congress Lok Sabha MP Manish Tewari called the situation a "flagrant breach of parliamentary conventions". In a post on X on November 21, he said the longest gap between adjournment sine die and prorogation in earlier Lok Sabhas was 28 days. He tagged Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in the post.

There is no official explanation for the delay, NDTV reported. Opposition leaders including Jairam Ramesh have alleged it is linked to securing numbers for a delimitation or women's reservation Bill. NDTV said these are allegations and that no evidence has been presented publicly. It added that some media reports cite unnamed sources saying key legislation is being prepared.
NDTV also noted that Winter Sessions have increasingly started in December. Four of the last eight began that month, against three between 2000 and 2016.
keyFacts: The Monsoon Session was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026.
As of November 23, the gap stood at 103 days against a 25-year average of about 95.
The Winter Session has been skipped four times, according to The Hindu.
Parliament has not been prorogued, and Manish Tewari says earlier gaps were at most 28 days.
stories.background: Parliament usually meets in three sessions a year: Budget, Monsoon and Winter. Winter Sessions were historically convened in the second half of November, though December starts have become more common in recent years, NDTV reported. The Winter Session did not take place in 2020 because of the pandemic.
stories.whyItMatters: The timing of the session determines when Parliament can take up legislation, including the delimitation Bill that The Hindu says is the subject of speculation.

stories.headline: Bengal to rename itself Paschim Banga in English; land law changes planned
stories.dek: Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said eight bills will come up in a December session, and the cabinet raised the monthly allowance for unemployed graduates to ₹2,000.
stories.summary: West Bengal's cabinet cleared plans to bring a bill on December 9 changing the state's English name to Paschim Banga. Eight bills are lined up for the session, including amendments to the land reforms law to ease acquisition for industry.
body: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Monday that his government will table a bill on December 9 to change the state's English name from West Bengal to Paschim Banga, after a cabinet meeting at Nabanna, the state secretariat.

The winter session of the Assembly will run from December 4 to 14, and the government plans to introduce eight bills. Adhikari said the animal husbandry, panchayat and rural development, refugee rehabilitation, labour, mass education and finance departments are among those presenting them.
"The Bengali name will be written in English alphabet once the bill is passed," Adhikari told the media.

One of the eight bills will amend the land reforms law to ease land acquisition for industry, official sources told reporters. Others relate to MSMEs and ease of doing business. Details of the land amendments are not yet known. Sources said the government does not plan to scrap the land ceiling.

Industry Minister Tapas Roy said he could share details once the bill reaches him. "Land pooling is a different matter, and the amendments may not include it," he said, while confirming the changes would try to ease land-related hurdles for industrial growth.

Adhikari has said the government will neither forcibly acquire land from farmers nor leave industry to buy land on its own. He expects to acquire 8,000 to 10,000 acres in the short term through the West Bengal Industrial Development Corporation, including in Singur.

The cabinet also approved a monthly allowance of ₹2,000 from January for unemployed graduates and diploma holders from government vocational institutions and ITIs under the Bhorsha Karmasuchi scheme. Unemployed non-graduates will receive ₹1,500. Beneficiaries must be aged 21 to 45, and a family can have at most two.

Adhikari said the amounts would rise to ₹3,000 and ₹2,000 respectively from 2028-29, as promised in the BJP manifesto. He said verification of 54 lakh existing beneficiaries of the earlier Banglar Yuva Sathi scheme will be completed by December 31.

The cabinet further decided to give up to ₹1 lakh a month to individuals or institutions caring for aged cows, and to raise the daily meal budget for physically challenged residents of state-run homes from ₹56 to ₹110. Adhikari also said the state electricity distribution company will move to monthly billing.
Hindustan Times reported that no faction of the Trinamool Congress had commented on the announcements by 5pm. The Bhorsha Karmasuchi scheme will be formally launched at an event in February.
keyFacts: The renaming bill is due to be tabled in the Assembly on December 9.
The winter session runs from December 4 to 14, with eight bills planned.
Unemployed graduates will get ₹2,000 a month from January 2027; non-graduates ₹1,500.
The cabinet approved 10,146 fresh recruitments, most in the Home Department.
The West Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955, caps agricultural holdings at about 17.30 acres per family.
stories.background:
The names West Bengal and Paschim Banga date to the 1947 Partition, when the eastern part of the undivided Bengal province became East Pakistan. Bengalis continued to call it East Bengal and Purba Banga.

The BJP came to power in West Bengal in May. Bhorsha Karmasuchi replaces the Trinamool government's Banglar Yuva Sathi scheme, announced by Mamata Banerjee in February.
stories.whyItMatters: Unemployed graduates in the state will receive a higher monthly allowance from January, and the proposed land amendments could change how industry acquires land in West Bengal.

stories.headline: China says it is ready to work with India on business visas
stories.dek: A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson responded to reports that Chinese missions have cut visa issuance to Indians, including business visas.
stories.summary: China said on Monday it stands ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel of both sides. The statement followed reports that Chinese missions had reduced visas issued to Indian nationals.
body: China said on Monday it is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both countries, after reports that Chinese diplomatic missions have reduced visa issuance to Indian nationals.

A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson made the remarks in a written reply to questions from PTI. "China issues visas for eligible foreign nationals coming to China in accordance with laws and regulations," the spokesperson said. "We stand ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel of both sides."

The reports, as relayed by PTI, said fewer Indian businessmen were granted visas to attend this month's China International Import Expo in Shanghai. The annual trade fair brings together companies from around the world to show their products to Chinese consumers.

Beijing has also stopped the China Visa Application Centre, a service provider, from accepting visa applications, according to the reports. Chinese missions now handle applications directly, as demand for Chinese visas, particularly business visas, has risen.

Asked about the state of bilateral ties after a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September, the spokesperson said the two leaders had reached a key understanding. "The most important common understanding they (Modi and Xi) reached is that China and India need to be partners. Both sides are working to deliver on this important common understanding," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that China "stands ready to work with India to improve and grow bilateral relations, support each other's development and revitalisation, and contribute to world peace and prosperity".
The statement did not directly address the reported reductions or say whether any change in visa practice was planned.
keyFacts: A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson replied in writing to PTI questions on Monday.

India resumed tourist visas for Chinese nationals in July last year after a five-year gap.

stories.background:
Ties between the two countries came under severe strain after the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. India resumed issuing tourist visas to Chinese nationals in July last year, and the two sides have since restored direct flights between several cities, including Beijing and New Delhi.

China's embassy in India launched an online visa application system for Indian applicants in December last year.

stories.headline: Nifty falls 1.75%, its sharpest drop since July; markets shut on Tuesday
stories.dek: Exchanges are closed on Tuesday for Guru Nanak Jayanti, and analysts said a rebound in US technology shares could weigh on Indian equities when trading resumes on Wednesday.
stories.summary: The Nifty 50 fell 1.75% on Monday, its steepest one-day drop since July 8, after a four-week rally. The Sensex lost 1,483.72 points, and BSE and NSE trading is suspended on Tuesday.
body: The Nifty 50 fell 1.75% to 25,349.65 on Monday, its steepest one-day drop since July 8, as investors booked profits after a four-week rally; the Sensex lost 1.77%.

The 30-share Sensex shed 1,483.72 points to close at 82,435.99. Mint reported that the fall wiped ₹5.17 trillion off the market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies. The index had opened higher but lost its early gains and touched an intraday low of 82,395.88.

Before Monday, the Nifty 50 had risen nearly 14%, helped by foreign inflows of over ₹1 trillion, a stronger rupee and a sell-off in the global artificial intelligence theme, Mint reported. The index ended 3.9% below its all-time high of 26,373.2, against 2.2% on Friday. It now needs to gain 650 points to reach 26,000.

All sectoral indices except Nifty IT, Nifty Consumer and Nifty Realty ended lower. The Nifty Metal index fell 3.6%, with Tata Steel down 8.4% after it announced plans to acquire Apollo Tubes. The Nifty Bank index fell 3.2%. Axis Bank lost 3.95%, ICICI Bank 3.39%, HDFC Bank 3.22%, SBI 2.91% and Kotak Mahindra Bank 2.52%.

IT shares gained. TCS rose 3.47%, Tech Mahindra 2.13%, HCL Technologies 1.94% and Infosys 0.70%. Provisional NSE data showed foreign institutional investors were net buyers of ₹5,672 crore, while domestic institutions sold a net ₹2,760 crore.
Most Asian markets also fell. Japan's Nikkei 225 declined 5.06% and South Korea's Kospi 3.78%, while Taiwan's Taiex rose 2.16%.

US stocks rose sharply on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, Mint reported. As of 10.20 pm India time, the S&P 500 was up 5% and the Nasdaq composite up 6.9%. A market expert quoted by Mint said Huang returned 11 days after resigning.

Prabhakar Kudva of Samvitti Capital said that if US tech-heavy indices sustain their recovery over the next few sessions, Indian markets could give back some recent gains. IIFL group founder Nirmal Jain said the Nifty would stay sideways with an upside bias, as global investors diversify into markets such as India.

Nagaraj Shetti of HDFC Securities said the day's action points to a short-term downside reversal pattern, to be confirmed only if weakness persists in the next session. Shrikant Chouhan of Kotak Neo said the market fell more than 640 points from the day's high for the Nifty and 2,250 for the Sensex, forming a long bearish candle that suggests further correction.
The BSE and NSE are closed on Tuesday, November 24, for Guru Nanak Jayanti. Trading resumes on Wednesday.

stories.background:
Foreign institutional investors have been net buyers of Indian equities since October 28, after a sell-off in AI-heavy indices globally. They have bought a net ₹1.3 trillion since then, according to NSDL data cited by Mint. The Nifty had ended Friday 199 points short of 26,000.

November 24 is the second-last stock market holiday of 2026. The exchanges will next be shut on December 25 for Christmas.
stories.whyItMatters: Analysts quoted by Mint said a sustained recovery in US technology stocks could draw investors away from India, whose recent rally was partly driven by money moving out of AI-linked shares.

stories.headline: Indonesia candy factory fire death toll rises to 26, rescuers search for missing
stories.dek: Firefighters were still cooling debris at the Banten Province site on Monday, and authorities have not yet established what caused the blaze.
stories.summary: Indonesian authorities raised the death toll from a weekend fire at a candy factory in Banten Province to 26, while rescuers continued to look for dozens of missing workers. The cause of the blaze, which began on Saturday, is under investigation.
body: Indonesian authorities have raised to 26 the number of people killed in a fire at a candy factory in Banten Province, with rescuers still searching for dozens of workers reported missing, according to the assignment's latest figures.

Reports published on Monday carried a lower toll. The New York Times quoted police as saying 24 people had died, and the South China Morning Post said Indonesia confirmed 24 deaths and that about 30 people were still missing.

The fire broke out on Saturday at the Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Serang, in the Cikande area, about 50 kilometres from the capital, Jakarta. The Times reported it started in the afternoon and burned for hours. The South China Morning Post described the start as Saturday evening. The sources differ on the timing.

The company makes milk candies and lollipops sold under the Milkita brand. It said 300 people were inside the factory compound on Saturday, and that 65 were believed to be in the area where the fire started.

Two days after the blaze, firefighters were still cooling the charred debris of the two-storey building because of concerns that fires could reignite, the Times reported. Part of the roof had caved in. The South China Morning Post said rescuers were working through unstable structures in the burned wreckage.

Rescue workers in masks were seen carrying black body bags out of the building. Bags containing human remains were sent to hospitals for identification, and police said dozens of family members had given DNA samples.
Said Iqbal, an adviser to President Prabowo Subianto on labour, visited the site on Monday. Authorities are still investigating the cause of the fire.
keyFacts: Death toll stands at 26, according to the latest figures; earlier reports said 24.

The company said 300 people were in the compound and 65 in the affected area.
About 30 people were reported missing as of Monday, according to the South China Morning Post.
Dozens of relatives have given DNA samples to help identify remains, police said.

stories.headline: Strike halts flights and public transport across Belgium as tens of thousands march
stories.dek: Prime Minister Bart De Wever set a year-end deadline for his coalition to agree a budget, France 24 reported, as unions protested planned spending cuts.
stories.summary: A national strike against planned austerity measures stopped air traffic at Brussels Airport and Charleroi and disrupted public transport on Monday. Tens of thousands marched in Brussels while the prime minister's coalition remained split over a budget.
body: A national strike against planned austerity measures halted all air traffic at Brussels Airport and Charleroi and disrupted public transport across Belgium on Monday, while tens of thousands of people marched through Brussels.

No flights took off or landed at Brussels Airport in Zaventem between 07:00 and 21:00 local time because of a strike by air traffic controllers. Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said 404 flights could not be operated, affecting more than 50,000 passengers.

At Charleroi, which hosts low-cost carriers such as Ryanair, all flights were shown as "scheduled" regardless of departure or arrival time, the BBC reported. One passenger told broadcaster RTBF she had received no warning and learned there were no flights only on reaching the airport.

Florence Faure, a French passenger who had flown in from Beijing, told Reuters her connection to Paris Charles de Gaulle was cancelled. "Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.
Underground services in Brussels were halted. Schools and other public services also faced disruption.
Philippe Naime, a teacher who joined the march, told Reuters: "Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves."

Bert Engelaar, head of the FGTB union, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system". He called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes". Ann Vermorgen of the CSC union criticised plans to cut bank holidays that fall on weekends.

De Wever leads a five-party coalition. One member, the socialist Vooruit, has refused to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants higher taxes on the rich and smaller cuts to pensions and health.

De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse began. The royal palace said the king regretted the lack of significant progress and urged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible.
France 24 reported that De Wever set a new year-end deadline for the coalition to agree a cost-cutting budget or face collapse.

stories.background: King Philippe declined Prime Minister Bart De Wever's resignation earlier in November, giving him more time to negotiate a budget aimed at cutting borrowing costs. A series of strikes has hit Belgium in recent months over the plans.
stories.whyItMatters: Travellers faced mass cancellations, and the government must settle a budget dispute by the year-end deadline or risk collapse.

stories.headline: Mexican soldiers fired on after arrest of cartel leader Meza Flores
stories.dek: Mexico says the operation was planned and led by its own forces, with US intelligence but no American agents on the ground.
stories.summary: Eight suspected cartel members were detained after soldiers were shot at in Sinaloa state, days after the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. President Claudia Sheinbaum said US agents took no part in the operation.
body: Mexican soldiers detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel on Sunday after coming under fire on patrol in Sinaloa de Leyva, in Sinaloa state, the defence ministry said. The attack followed the arrest of the group's leader, Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro".

The ministry said the soldiers were trying to restore order when they were shot at. It said the eight had also taken part in retaliatory violence after the arrest, and that one of them was under age. Special forces seized six vehicles, two of them armoured and fitted with gun turrets.

Sources differ on the day of the arrest. The BBC and the New York Times place it on Friday; Bloomberg says Saturday. Elite Mexican forces took Meza Flores after heavy gunfire around his compound in Sinaloa.

At her morning press conference on Monday, President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexican forces planned and led the operation. "The areas in which we coordinate with the US are security and intelligence. That was the agreement we reached from the start," she said. "But they do not conduct operations in Mexico." She confirmed that Mexican officials had asked the US to deploy a drone to help, without giving details.

Defence Minister Ricardo Trevilla said security forces killed 16 alleged associates of Meza Flores and detained another 16. Four soldiers died and ten federal agents were injured, he said. Hundreds of troops, special forces and several Black Hawk helicopters were mobilised. Officials had first reported seven suspected gang members dead before more bodies were found.

The US Department of Justice called the arrest "a spectacular military operation" and said the Homeland Security Task Force supported the Mexican military. US Ambassador Ronald Johnson pointed to intelligence sharing in a post on X. Washington has not claimed responsibility for the operation.

Meza Flores, 44, was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list, and the US had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest or conviction. He faces extradition to the US. US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva called him "the most dangerous man in Mexico".
According to the US Treasury, his Guasave Cartel has trafficked drugs into the US since at least 2000 and has recently fought a turf war with a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel.
keyFacts: Eight suspected cartel members were detained on Sunday after soldiers were shot at in Sinaloa de Leyva.

stories.background:
Sheinbaum has faced pressure from US President Donald Trump to act more forcefully against cartels. After meeting her in China last week, Trump repeated that cartels are "running Mexico", which she rejects. Sheinbaum has said she will work with US authorities as long as Mexican sovereignty is respected.

The arrest is Mexico's highest-profile cartel operation since February, when Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera, leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, died of injuries after a military raid, according to Bloomberg.
stories.whyItMatters: The arrest and the violence that followed test Mexico's approach of working with US intelligence while keeping operations under Mexican command.
